descripcion: At C2 you handle three-part phrasal verbs and the ones with a figurative meaning that has drifted far from their literal parts: come up against, get away with, look down on. Their idiomatic sense must be learned as a fixed unit; the literal words no longer help.

ejemplos.texto: The proposal came up against fierce resistance from the board.
He somehow got away with it, against all odds.
She never looked down on anyone, regardless of their background.

notas: The three parts of these verbs never separate, unlike the two-part verbs common at lower levels.
The figurative meaning is now fully detached from the literal words — look down on has nothing to do with physical height.
These verbs are frequent in speech and informal writing but sound wrong translated literally into a formal register.

contraste.es: El español carece de esta clase de verbo compuesto y suele necesitar una frase entera para el mismo matiz (salirse con la suya, mirar por encima del hombro). Los hispanohablantes de C2 entienden estos verbos al leerlos, pero rara vez los producen activamente sin práctica dirigida.

errores: Trying to split a three-part phrasal verb, which never happens.
Interpreting the verb literally instead of by its drifted figurative sense.
Using a three-part phrasal verb in a register too formal for it.

traducciones.de: auf etwas stoßen / mit etwas konfrontiert werden
sich etwas einfangen / an etwas erkranken

autochequeo: Have I kept every three-part verb unsplit?
Does the meaning match the figurative sense, not the literal words?
Does the register fit an informal or neutral context, not a very formal one?
Have I used at least four different three-part verbs?
Would a native speaker recognise this as natural, idiomatic English?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on advanced three-part phrasal verbs. Check that they remain unsplit and that the figurative meaning is used correctly. Do not rewrite the text.
